text: In sixteen thirty-seven, a single Dutch flower bulb could sell for as much as a house.
sub: In 1637, a single Dutch flower bulb could sell for as much as a house.

text: Not gold. Not diamonds. A tulip.

text: Tulips had come from the Ottoman Empire, and the Dutch fell in love with them.

text: The rarest ones had flames of colour across their petals. And no one could predict which bulb would bloom like that.

text: They traded in taverns, through the winter, while the bulbs were still in the ground. Buying flowers nobody had seen.

text: Prices doubled. Then doubled again. People bought, just to sell a week later, for more.

text: The most famous bulb of all, the Semper Augustus, was said to be worth a mansion.

text: And then, in February sixteen thirty-seven, at a sale in Haarlem, the buyers stayed away.

text: Within days, the panic spread. Prices collapsed. People refused to pay for bulbs they had promised to buy.

text: For centuries, it was told as the story of a country ruined. But few people actually went broke. What really broke was trust.
